title: THE WOMAN THEY MOCKED FOR HAVING NO CHILDREN… LATER HELD SIX CHILDREN IN HER STORY. BUT THE GREATEST MIRACLE WASN’T WHAT GOD PUT IN HER ARMS.
paragraphs: THE WOMAN THEY MOCKED FOR HAVING NO CHILDREN… LATER HELD SIX CHILDREN IN HER STORY. BUT THE GREATEST MIRACLE WASN’T WHAT GOD PUT IN HER ARMS.

They laughed at her empty womb. They watched her cry. They never imagined that the woman who once prayed through unbearable humiliation would become the mother of a prophet—and that her greatest act of faith would happen before five more children were born.
“And the LORD visited Hannah, so that she conceived, and bare three sons and two daughters. And the child Samuel grew before the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:21 (KJV)
There is a kind of pain that doesn't leave bruises.
You can dress beautifully, smile at people, attend worship, sit at the family table, and still feel like something inside you is quietly falling apart.
And sometimes the cruelest part isn't even what you're missing.
It's the people who keep reminding you.
Hannah knew that kind of pain.

She knew what it felt like to watch someone else receive what she had begged God for. She knew the exhausting humiliation of carrying a longing that everybody seemed to notice but nobody truly understood.
And she knew what it was like to pray for something year after year while heaven appeared silent.
But there is something about Hannah's story that many people miss.
Before God gave her five more children, He asked her to release the one child she had spent years begging Him to give her.
Read that again.
Because the deepest part of this story isn't simply about a barren woman becoming a mother.
It's about a wounded woman who learned to trust God with the very thing she feared losing most.
And somewhere in her story, you might recognize your own.
Maybe you're not praying for a child.
Maybe you're praying for a marriage that seems beyond repair.
A son who no longer speaks to you.
A daughter who has walked away from God.
A diagnosis you wish the doctor had never spoken.
A business that collapsed after years of sacrifice.
A relationship that ended without an explanation.
Or a second chance you secretly believe you no longer deserve.
You have watched other people celebrate answers to prayers that sound painfully similar to yours.
You congratulated them.
You smiled for the photograph.
You even whispered, "Praise God."
Then you went home, closed the door, and wondered why your own life still felt so empty.
If you've ever lived through that moment, stay with Hannah.
Because Scripture doesn't introduce her as a woman who had everything figured out.
It introduces her as a woman whose heart was breaking.
And God did not overlook her.
Hannah was married to Elkanah, a man who had two wives: Hannah and Peninnah.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
That single difference became a source of deep suffering.
First Samuel 1:5 tells us that Elkanah loved Hannah, yet the LORD had closed her womb.
Notice how carefully Scripture holds those two truths together.
She was loved.
And she was suffering.
Being loved did not automatically remove her pain.
Having a husband who cared for her did not erase the longing she carried.
And although the biblical narrative records that God had closed her womb, it does not say Hannah was being punished for a secret sin.
That distinction matters.
Because some people have been wounded by the terrible suggestion that every unanswered prayer is evidence of weak faith, hidden disobedience, or divine rejection.
But Hannah's story gives us no permission to condemn people that way.
Infertility was not proof that Hannah was worthless.
Her suffering was not evidence that she was less loved.
And her inability to conceive did not make her less of a woman.
Yet Peninnah treated Hannah's pain like an opportunity.
The Bible says:
“And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb.” — 1 Samuel 1:6 (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated "provoked" comes from the root כעס (kaʿas), associated with provoking, vexing, or causing distress.
This wasn't harmless teasing.
The text describes deliberate provocation.
Peninnah knew where Hannah was hurting.
And she kept pressing the wound.
Imagine sitting at a family gathering while another woman makes sure you notice her children.
Imagine trying to eat while the thing you most deeply desire is being used to humiliate you.
Imagine being reminded, again and again, that you have not received what someone else possesses.
And then imagine being expected to remain pleasant.
Scripture tells us that this continued year after year.
Not once.
Not during one unfortunate conversation.
Year after year.
Until Hannah wept and could not eat.
Some wounds become especially exhausting because they are reopened before they have time to heal.
And sometimes the people closest to you don't understand how deep those wounds have become.
Elkanah asked Hannah:
“Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?” — 1 Samuel 1:8 (KJV)
He loved her.
But his question also reveals something painfully human.
Sometimes people genuinely love us and still don't understand our grief.
They offer explanations when we need compassion.
They try to solve what we are still struggling to express.
They remind us of everything we have when we are grieving something we don't.
Perhaps you've heard it yourself.
"You should be grateful."
"Other people have it worse."
"Just move on."
"Stop thinking about it."
"Maybe it's not meant for you."
And although some of those words may be spoken with good intentions, they can land heavily on an already exhausted heart.
Hannah wasn't ungrateful because she grieved.
She was human.
And the God who created her did not require her to pretend otherwise.
One day, after eating and drinking at Shiloh, Hannah rose and went before the LORD.
The Bible describes her condition with devastating simplicity:
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.” — 1 Samuel 1:10 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is מָרַת נָפֶשׁ (marat nefesh), meaning bitter or deeply distressed in soul.
This wasn't a polished religious performance.
This wasn't a woman trying to impress the people around her.
This was someone carrying anguish she could no longer contain.
And where did she bring it?
To God.
Not because she had stopped hurting.
But because she knew where to take her hurt.
There is a difference between pretending to be strong and bringing your weakness before the Lord.
Hannah did not wait until she could pray beautifully.
She prayed while broken.
She did not wait until her emotions became manageable.
She came while overwhelmed.
She did not need an audience.
She needed God.
And perhaps that is where some of us need to return.
Not to another argument.
Not to another attempt to prove our worth.
Not to another exhausting performance of being okay.
But to the presence of the Father, where even the prayers we struggle to speak are known.
Hannah made a vow that if God gave her a son, she would give that son to the LORD for his lifetime.
Then something remarkable happened.
Eli the priest saw her lips moving, but he heard no voice.
And he misunderstood her.
He thought she was drunk.
Imagine that.
She had already endured humiliation at home.
Now, in the very place where she came seeking God, she was misjudged by a spiritual leader.
There are people reading this who know exactly how that feels.
You finally gather enough courage to speak about your pain, and someone misunderstands you.
You seek help, and someone questions your character.
You come to worship carrying grief, and someone assumes the worst.
But Hannah answered with extraordinary honesty:
“No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 1:15 (KJV)
"I have poured out my soul."
What a description of prayer.
Not impressive language.
Not carefully rehearsed sentences.
Not spiritual vocabulary designed to sound mature.
Just a soul being poured out before God.
And that is still an invitation available to us through Jesus Christ.

Hebrews 4:15–16 tells us that we have a High Priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses and that we may approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace in our time of need.
Hannah approached God under the old covenant.
We come to the Father through Jesus Christ, our crucified and risen High Priest.
And because of Him, our suffering does not have to remain hidden behind religious appearances.
You can come honestly.
You can confess your fear.
You can admit your anger without making anger your master.
You can acknowledge your disappointment without pretending God has abandoned His throne.
You can say, "Lord, I believe. Help my unbelief."
And you can weep.
Tears do not automatically mean your faith has failed.
Sometimes tears are simply what happens when a burdened heart finally stops pretending.
After Eli blessed Hannah, Scripture records something significant.
She went away, ate, and her face was no longer sad as before.
Her circumstances had not yet changed.
She had not yet conceived.
She was not holding a baby.
No visible miracle had taken place.
Yet something had shifted.
The text doesn't give us permission to claim that Hannah suddenly knew every detail of what God would do.
But it does show that she left that encounter differently from how she arrived.
And that matters.
Because sometimes the first evidence of God's work in a painful season isn't that the situation changes immediately.
Sometimes it is that you find enough strength to face another day.
Not because the outcome is guaranteed to be what you want.
But because the Lord remains worthy of your trust.
Then came the moment Hannah had waited for.
“And the LORD remembered her.” — 1 Samuel 1:19 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the expression is וַיִּזְכְּרֶהָ יְהוָה (vayyizkereha YHWH).
The verb comes from זכר (zakhar), "to remember."
This does not mean God had forgotten Hannah's existence and suddenly recalled her.
In biblical narrative, divine remembering frequently signals God's purposeful attention and action in accordance with His will.
God had not lost track of her.
And in the unfolding of His purpose, He acted.
Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son.
She named him Samuel.

First Samuel 1:20 connects his name with her testimony that she had asked him of the LORD. The precise linguistic derivation of the name is debated, but the narrative's theological emphasis is unmistakable.
This child was received as an answer to prayer.
Imagine the moment.
The woman who once sat unable to eat now holding a newborn.
The woman who had been mocked now hearing the cries of her own child.
The woman who had poured out her soul now whispering over a life she had once only imagined.
Perhaps she touched his tiny fingers.
Perhaps she watched him sleep and remembered those long years of unanswered prayer.
Scripture does not describe those private moments, so we cannot claim to know them.
But anyone who has waited through profound grief can understand why this birth mattered.
Samuel was not merely the arrival of something Hannah wanted.
He was a living reminder of God's mercy toward her.
And yet this is where the story becomes more challenging than the familiar testimony of a long-awaited blessing.
Because Hannah remembered her vow.
She had promised to give Samuel to the LORD.
And she kept her word.
After Samuel was weaned, Hannah brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh.
She told Eli:

“For this child I prayed; and the LORD hath given me my petition which I asked of him: Therefore also I have lent him to the LORD; as long as he liveth he shall be lent to the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 1:27–28 (KJV)

The Hebrew verb in verse 28 is connected to שאל (shaʾal), meaning "to ask" or "request." The wording creates a deliberate relationship between Hannah asking God for Samuel and dedicating Samuel to Him.
The English word "lent" in the King James Version should not be misunderstood as an ordinary temporary loan.
Hannah was dedicating her son to the LORD for his lifetime, as her vow had promised.
Think about the weight of that.
She had waited years.
She had endured ridicule.
She had cried until she could not eat.
She had begged God for a child.
And now, having received him, she brought him back to the place of worship.
Not because she didn't love him.
But because she recognized that the child she loved belonged ultimately to God.
This is not a command that parents today must surrender their children to religious institutions.
Nor does it mean God requires believers to give away whatever brings them joy.
Hannah's vow was particular to her circumstances.
But the spiritual question beneath her obedience reaches across generations.
Do we love God's gifts more than we love God?
Can we receive a blessing with gratitude without turning it into the center of our identity?
Can we trust the Lord even when obedience costs us something precious?
That is where Hannah's faith becomes deeply convicting.
She did not simply praise God when she received Samuel.
She worshiped God when she gave Samuel back.
And her worship was not the end of her story.
It was the beginning of another chapter.
First Samuel 2 records Hannah's extraordinary prayer of praise.
She rejoiced in the LORD, not merely in her changed circumstances.
She declared:
“The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up.” — 1 Samuel 2:7 (KJV)
Her song celebrated God's holiness, sovereignty, justice, and power to reverse human circumstances.
It also looked beyond her personal experience.
The final verse speaks of the LORD giving strength to His king and exalting the horn of His anointed.
The Hebrew word for "anointed" is מְשִׁיחוֹ (meshicho), meaning "his anointed one," from the root משח (mashach), "to anoint."
This is the same Hebrew word family from which the title Messiah comes.
In its immediate context, Hannah's prayer anticipates God's work through kingship in Israel, a theme that unfolds prominently through Samuel's ministry and the rise of David.
Within the full biblical story, the hope associated with God's anointed King ultimately finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
That connection matters.
Because Hannah's story was never intended to stop with Hannah.
Her son Samuel would grow to become a prophet and judge in Israel.
He would play a central role in the transition to Israel's monarchy.
He would anoint David, whose royal line becomes central to the biblical promises concerning the Messiah.
And the New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the promised Son of David.
The woman who was humiliated over her childlessness became the mother of a man whose ministry would help shape a pivotal chapter in Israel's redemptive history.
But don't miss the greater truth.
Samuel was important.
Jesus is greater.
Samuel served as a prophet.
Jesus is the ultimate revelation of the Father.
Samuel participated in the story of Israel's kings.
Jesus is the eternal King.
Samuel's life helped prepare the way for events that would unfold across generations.
Jesus came to accomplish what no prophet, priest, or earthly king could accomplish through human effort.
He came to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life are offered to everyone who repents and believes the Gospel.
Hannah's story shows us a God who hears the cries of the afflicted.
The Gospel reveals how far that same God went to rescue the lost.
And that brings us to the verse that makes Hannah's story so unforgettable.
“And the LORD visited Hannah, so that she conceived, and bare three sons and two daughters. And the child Samuel grew before the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:21 (KJV)
Three sons.
Two daughters.
Five more children after Samuel.
Six children in total.
The Hebrew text begins:
כִּי־פָקַד יְהוָה אֶת־חַנָּה
Ki-faqad YHWH et-Channah.
A contextually faithful translation is:
“For the LORD visited Hannah.”
The verb פָּקַד (paqad) has a range of meanings depending on context, including to attend to, visit, appoint, or take action concerning someone.
Here, the surrounding verse explains the nature of that divine visitation.
God graciously acted toward Hannah, and she conceived and bore additional children.
This was not a casual visit.
It was God's active intervention in the life of a woman whose suffering had occupied the opening chapter of the book.
And the number matters because Scripture explicitly records it.
Three additional sons.
Two daughters.
Five more children.
But there is something we must be careful not to do with this beautiful passage.
We must not turn Hannah's blessing into a universal formula.
The Bible does not teach that every woman struggling with infertility will eventually conceive if she prays long enough.
It does not promise that surrendering one blessing will automatically produce five more.
It does not teach that faithful giving obligates God to multiply our possessions, heal every illness, restore every relationship, or fulfill every earthly desire.
God's gracious action toward Hannah was real.
But it was not a contract that places the Almighty under our control.
Some faithful women never bear biological children.
Some faithful couples endure infertility throughout their lives.
Some people die still waiting for an earthly answer to a deeply cherished prayer.
And none of those realities makes them less loved by Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not promise that every sorrow will be reversed before we leave this world.
It promises something greater: that through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, sin and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Revelation 21:4 points toward the day when God will wipe away every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is the ultimate restoration toward which every earthly mercy points.
And until that day, we live by faith.
Not by pretending every wound has healed.
Not by insisting every story must end the way Hannah's did.
But by holding fast to the One who died and rose again.
There is another detail in Hannah's story that deserves attention.
After Samuel was dedicated to the LORD, his mother did not simply disappear from his life.
First Samuel 2:19 tells us that Hannah made him a little coat and brought it to him year by year when she came with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
A little coat.
Such an ordinary detail.
And yet it carries enormous tenderness.
The prophet who would one day speak God's word to Israel was once a little boy whose mother brought him clothing.
Year after year.
As he grew.
Imagine those garments changing in size.
The little boy growing taller.
His mother preparing another coat.
Her love continuing through an unusual arrangement of separation and dedication.
The Bible does not tell us everything Hannah felt during those visits.
But it does tell us she remained involved in this tangible way.
Her obedience did not erase her motherhood.
Her dedication did not cancel her love.
And God's work through Samuel did not make the ordinary tenderness of a mother insignificant.
Then, in the same passage that records Eli blessing Elkanah and Hannah, we read that the LORD visited Hannah and she bore more children.
The woman who had once been repeatedly humiliated because she had no children was now the mother of six.
But notice what Scripture does not record.
It does not tell us that Hannah went back to Peninnah to boast.
It does not describe Hannah humiliating the woman who had humiliated her.
It does not show Hannah making revenge the centerpiece of her testimony.
And we should not invent those scenes.
The narrative turns our attention instead toward the LORD and toward Samuel growing before Him.
That is a lesson worth carrying.
Sometimes when we've been wounded, we secretly imagine that healing will feel like finally proving everybody wrong.
We rehearse the conversations.
We imagine the faces.
We dream of the day when those who mocked us will have to admit they misjudged us.
And sometimes God does bring visible vindication.
But the deepest healing is not found in making your enemies feel small.
It is found in being made whole before God.
You do not have to become cruel because someone was cruel to you.
You do not have to make your success a weapon.
You do not have to turn your testimony into revenge.
In Christ, there is a better way.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending the harm never happened.
It does not require remaining in abusive situations or refusing appropriate boundaries.
But it does mean surrendering vengeance to God and refusing to let another person's cruelty become the ruler of your heart.
Romans 12:19 reminds believers that vengeance belongs to the Lord.
And Ephesians 4:32 calls us to forgive one another as God in Christ forgave us.
Perhaps that is the word someone needs today.
You have spent so long trying to prove that you matter.
Trying to prove that you are not a failure.
Trying to prove that your past doesn't define you.
Trying to prove that the people who rejected you made a mistake.
But what if your freedom begins when you stop allowing their judgment to determine your worth?
What if the cross of Jesus Christ has already answered the deepest question?
You are not saved because you finally became impressive.
You are not welcomed by God because your life now looks successful.
You are not forgiven because you managed to repair every consequence of your past.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the Savior who calls sinners to repentance does not merely polish their reputations.
He makes them new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that if anyone is in Christ, that person is a new creation.
That is why this story belongs so naturally within the testimony we keep proclaiming at Gospel Warrior.
Not because every painful story ends in public applause.
Not because every broken dream is restored exactly as we imagined.
Not because the world finally agrees that we were worthy all along.
But because Jesus Christ has the authority to redeem sinners, restore fellowship with God, and give eternal hope to people who could never save themselves.
Hannah's suffering was not itself a moral scandal, and her infertility was never a sin that required forgiveness.
We must never confuse suffering with guilt.
But her journey from public humiliation to worship and renewed blessing reminds us that the world's judgment is never the final measure of a person's life.
And the Gospel carries that truth into an even deeper reality.
The person everyone dismissed can be received by Christ.
The sinner who repents can be forgiven.
The ashamed can find mercy.
The proud can be humbled.
The brokenhearted can find comfort.
The spiritually lost can come home.
And no past is so powerful that it can overturn the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Maybe your story has been marked by decisions you regret.
Maybe there are things you wish you could erase.
Maybe you have spent years hiding behind a religious smile while your conscience quietly accuses you.
You know the Scriptures.
You know the worship songs.
You know how to say, "God is good."
But deep inside, you know there are places in your heart you have refused to surrender.
And perhaps Hannah's story has exposed something.
Not just your pain.
But your grip.
Your fear.
Your resentment.
Your need to control the outcome.
Your belief that God will only be good if He gives you exactly what you've asked for.
This is where the Gospel invites us into something more profound than simply receiving blessings.
It invites us to receive Christ Himself.
Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23 (KJV)
Following Jesus is not a transaction in which we surrender something small to guarantee something bigger.
It is a life of trusting the Savior who has already given Himself for us.
It is repentance.
It is grace.
It is learning to obey even when obedience is costly.
It is discovering that Christ is worthy when our prayers are answered and when we are still waiting.
And it is finding that the greatest gift God can give us is not an easier life.
It is reconciliation with Himself through His Son.
Hannah received Samuel.
Then she surrendered Samuel to the LORD.
Then God gave her five more children.
That is the sequence Scripture records.
But the spiritual beauty of her story is not that surrender became a technique for getting more.
It is that Hannah's worship was directed toward God, the Giver, not merely toward the gifts.
And maybe that is what makes her testimony so powerful.
She had learned to pour out her soul before the Lord.
She had learned to receive with gratitude.
She had learned to honor her vow.
And she had learned to praise the God whose purposes were greater than the circumstances that once threatened to crush her.
So now I want to speak to the person who has been quietly holding back tears while reading this.
You may not have Hannah's ending.
I cannot promise you that.
No faithful teacher of Scripture should promise you what God has not promised.
But I can point you to Hannah's God.
The God who is holy.
The God who hears.
The God who acts according to His wisdom.
The God who sees the afflicted.
The God who sent His Son into the world, not to save us from every temporary disappointment, but to save us from sin and death through His cross and resurrection.
And I can tell you this:
Your pain is not proof that your life is meaningless.
Your waiting is not proof that you have been abandoned.
Your past does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
And your worth is not determined by your fertility, marriage, income, reputation, accomplishments, or the approval of people who never understood what you were carrying.
Come to Jesus.
Not because He has promised to give you everything you want.
But because He is the Savior your soul needs.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come with the sins you need to confess and the wounds you can no longer pretend are healed.
Come with the prayer you've whispered a thousand times.
Come with the faith that feels smaller than it used to.
Come because He is merciful.
And if you already belong to Him, keep following.
Keep opening Scripture.
Keep praying.
Keep loving.
Keep obeying.
Keep bringing your burdens before the throne of grace.
Your life is not measured only by the answers you have received.
It is also being shaped by the One you are learning to trust.
And if this story has stirred something you haven't been able to say aloud, don't rush past that moment.
Be honest before God.
Perhaps you need to pray:

"Father, I have been carrying bitterness longer than I want to admit. I have compared my life with others. I have questioned Your goodness. I have wanted Your gifts more than I have wanted Your presence. Forgive me where I have sinned. Heal what is wounded. Teach me to trust You without trying to control You. Help me surrender what I cannot change and obey what You have clearly commanded. Thank You for Jesus Christ, who died for my sins and rose again. Draw me closer to Him. Let my life glorify You, whether I am rejoicing in an answered prayer or still learning to wait. In Jesus' name, amen."
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you don't need to pretend your heart is fine.
Maybe you simply need to bring it to God.
You do not have to explain your private pain publicly. Even a few words can invite brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you in prayer.
Your story may encourage someone who is struggling to believe they can keep going.
Someone reading this may be facing the same kind of grief you once carried.
Someone may be silently grieving infertility.
Someone may be recovering from humiliation, rejection, or years of unanswered prayer.
Someone may have begun to believe that their suffering means God has stopped loving them.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
But because the truth of God's Word deserves to travel beyond the people who already know it.
A friend who never comments may read it.
A relative who has stopped attending church may pause long enough to reconsider the Gospel.
Someone who has never opened a Bible may encounter the name of Jesus Christ through what you share.
We cannot know what God will do through one ordinary act of encouragement.
But we can be faithful with the opportunities in front of us.
Our desire is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ, encourage repentance and faith, and help believers become rooted in the Word of God.
We want those resources to help people read Scripture more carefully, understand the Gospel more deeply, and continue growing in Christ long after they finish a single article.
And I want to speak personally for a moment to those who have been strengthened by this ministry.

It is an opportunity to help sustain and expand the work: developing biblical teaching, preparing discipleship resources, maintaining access to free materials, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
At the same time, we want to be faithful to Scripture.
And if God has given you both the desire and the ability to help sustain this work, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us.
These products are reminders and resources for everyday faith, but they are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
Jesus Christ is.
Because one day, the articles we wrote will be forgotten.
The pages we built will fade.
The products we made will wear out.
The numbers that people celebrate online will no longer matter.
But the Word of the Lord endures forever.
And a life reconciled to God through Jesus Christ has a hope that reaches beyond the grave.
So before you leave, remember Hannah one last time.
Remember the woman who wept until she could not eat.
Remember the woman whose pain became another person's weapon.
Remember the woman who poured out her soul before the LORD.
Remember the mother who received a son and faithfully dedicated him to God.
Remember the five additional children Scripture records.
And above all, remember the God to whom she prayed.
The same holy God who ruled over Hannah's story has revealed His saving grace to us through Jesus Christ.
Your circumstances may be different.
Your answer may be different.
Your journey may be longer than you ever imagined.
But the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Repent.
Believe in Jesus Christ.
Rest in His finished work.

And entrust your life to the Savior whose grace is greater than your sin, whose resurrection is stronger than death, and whose faithfulness does not depend on whether your earthly story unfolds the way you hoped.
The world may remember what was missing from your life, but in Christ, what was missing never has the authority to define who you are.
